item.title: Estudio dirigido por NASA revela que algunos microorganismos terrestres podrían sobrevivir en la Luna
item.description: La Luna es un lugar inhóspito para las personas y otros organismos vivos de la Tierra, debido a la falta de aire respirable, las temperaturas extremas y la exposición a la implacable radiación espacial y a las partículas energéticas. Por eso los astronautas llevan trajes espaciales y las naves espaciales están equipadas con blindaje.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham
item.content:encoded: La Luna es un lugar inhóspito para las personas y otros organismos vivos de la Tierra, debido a la falta de aire respirable, las temperaturas extremas y la exposición a la implacable radiación espacial y a las partículas energéticas. Por eso los astronautas llevan trajes espaciales y las naves espaciales están equipadas con blindaje. Pero, ¿qué ocurre con los microbios que, inevitablemente, viajarán de polizones con los astronautas durante la exploración espacial? Una nueva investigación dirigida por científicos de la NASA, que analizó cinco tipos de hongos y bacterias, indica que algunos de ellos podrían, de hecho, sobrevivir durante un tiempo en determinadas condiciones en la superficie lunar, un hallazgo que suscita preocupación por la transferencia involuntaria de vida a la Luna. Estos microbios se sometieron a pruebas en simulaciones de tres regiones cercanas al Polo Sur lunar —el cráter Nobile, la Cresta de Conexión y el cráter de Gerlache— utilizando condiciones ambientales basadas en observaciones del Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter de la NASA y datos sobre la exposición a la radiación. Las simulaciones indicaron que algunos microbios podrían sobrevivir de semanas a meses en zonas como el interior de cráteres que están siempre en la sombra y durante estaciones concretas —otoño e invierno—, según el científico planetario Prabal Saxena, del Centro de Vuelos Espaciales Goddard de la NASA, en Maryland. Los dos hongos estudiados resultaron ser más resistentes que las tres especies de bacterias. El Aspergillus niger, una especie fúngica común que abunda en climas más cálidos y a la que a veces se denomina "moho negro", fue la más resistente. El Aspergillus prospera en lugares cálidos y húmedos, como los cuartos de baño y los sistemas de calefacción, ventilación y aire acondicionado. Los astronautas lo han encontrado en el interior de la Estación Espacial Internacional. Los experimentos han demostrado que puede incluso sobrevivir fuera de la estación mientras está en órbita. Los investigadores también estudiaron varias especies de Fusarium, un hongo común presente en el suelo. "El Aspergillus fue el más adecuado para sobrevivir en las regiones de los polos lunares. El Fusarium mostró una resistencia similar, aunque no en la misma medida que el Aspergillus", afirmó Saxena, autor principal del estudio publicado esta semana en la revista Science Advances. TRES ESPECIES DE BACTERIAS Se estudiaron tres especies de bacterias: Deinococcus radiodurans, un microbio del suelo conocido por soportar el frío y la radiación; Staphylococcus aureus, que suele encontrarse en la piel y en el interior de las fosas nasales; y Bacillus subtilis, presente en el suelo, la vegetación y el tracto gastrointestinal humano. "Las bacterias que examinamos eran menos resistentes a la radiación ultravioleta y, en consecuencia, presentaban una menor tasa de supervivencia, con el Deinococcus a la cabeza y el Staphylococcus y el Bacillus a la cola", explicó Saxena. La radiación ultravioleta y el calor —las temperaturas diurnas en la Luna pueden alcanzar unos 127 grados Celsius— fueron las mayores amenazas, junto con la radiación de partículas energéticas y los efectos del vacío natural en la superficie lunar. Los modelos revelaron mapas de "nichos de supervivencia" tan extensos como los fondos de cráteres de varios kilómetros de ancho. Según los modelos, el Aspergillus podría sobrevivir incluso en zonas expuestas a cierta luz solar y, por tanto, a la radiación ultravioleta. "Nuestro estudio se centró solo en la supervivencia de estas células, no en su crecimiento ni en su reproducción", explicó Heather Graham, geoquímica orgánica del Centro de Vuelos Espaciales Goddard y coautora del estudio. "Pero hay escenarios en los que las células pueden quedar enterradas, lo que las mantendría calientes y protegidas de la radiación. También podría haber situaciones en las que se formaran bolsas de agua líquida, lo que podría ayudar a los organismos a crecer", añadió Graham. Estos microbios podrían afectar a recursos como el agua —presente en forma de hielo en algunos lugares de la Luna— que son potencialmente útiles para los astronautas, según los investigadores. El estudio no analizó si las condiciones lunares podrían provocar mutaciones que hicieran que los microbios resultaran más peligrosos como patógenos. "El estudio se centró únicamente en la persistencia celular y no en las mutaciones, por lo que no podemos extrapolar estos resultados para incluir detalles sobre una futura patogenicidad", señaló Graham.

item.title: D.C. United transfer F Jacob Murrell to Scottish club
item.description: D.C. United transferred forward Jacob Murrell to Falkirk FC of the Scottish Premiership, the club announced Friday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: D.C. United transferred forward Jacob Murrell to Falkirk FC of the Scottish Premiership, the club announced Friday. Murrell, 22, joined D.C. as the No. 7 overall pick in the 2024 MLS SuperDraft and signed a three-year contract through 2026 with an option for 2027. The striker contributed four goals and five assists in 65 appearances across all competitions. As a rookie, he had one goal and three assists in 27 matches (six starts), plus three appearances in the 2024 Leagues Cup. Last year, he tallied two goals and one assist in 24 appearances in the regular season, plus one goal in two Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup appearances. He has come off the bench in eight games this season and has one assist. He played in one U.S. Open Cup match. "Jacob is a local talent who came to us as a first-round draft pick and grew into a professional over three seasons with this club," said managing director of soccer operations Erkut Sogut. "He gave this fanbase moments they will remember for a long time, and he earned everything he got here through his work." --Field Level Media

item.title: Seahawks WR Jake Bobo sustains 'serious' knee injury
item.description: Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Jake Bobo sustained a "serious" knee injury on Friday during a joint practice session with the Tennessee Titans in Nashville, head coach Mike Macdonald said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Jake Bobo sustained a "serious" knee injury on Friday during a joint practice session with the Tennessee Titans in Nashville, head coach Mike Macdonald said. "Our heart goes out to Jake Bobo," Macdonald said after the joint practice. "It seems like it's going to be a serious (right) knee (injury). We're going to get an image. But early returns, just looks like it's a long-term injury. That's unfortunate." Bobo was carted off the practice field after thrown a pass near the sideline. He played in 11 games last season and caught two passes on two targets for 20 yards. Bobo played on 17% of the offensive snaps (117) and 45% of special teams snaps (45). He made two catches in three playoff games for 33 yards and one TD for the Seahawks, who beat New England 29-13 in Super Bowl LX. For his career, Bobo has 34 receptions on 44 targets for 323 yards and three touchdowns in 45 regular-season games (three starts) since 2023. Bobo, 28, could have been a restricted free agent in the offseason when the Seahawks tendered a $3.5 million offer. The Jacksonville Jaguars signed him to an offer sheet on a two-year, $5.5 million deal, with $4.5 guaranteed, but Seattle matched the offer, per Spotrac.com. "He's a beast. He's just a great, great football player, a great Seahawk," Macdonald said. "Hopefully, (we) reflected that in our investment. We love him. We'll be there beside him as he recovers and pray for a speedy recovery. ... We said a prayer for him. Hate to see it." --Field Level Media

item.title: Uber defeats bid to dismiss racketeering lawsuit against California lawyers, doctors
item.description: A civil racketeering lawsuit brought by Uber alleging lawyers and doctors in California conspired to generate fraudulent injury claims is moving ahead after a judge refused to dismiss the case.
item.dc:creator: David Thomas
item.content:encoded: A civil racketeering lawsuit brought by Uber (UBER.N) alleging lawyers and doctors in California conspired to generate fraudulent injury claims is moving ahead after a judge refused to dismiss the case. U.S. District Judge Sherilyn Peace Garnett, in a ruling made public on Thursday, dismissed one claim Uber brought under the federal anti-racketeering law known as RICO – a conspiracy charge against all defendants – but kept the rideshare giant's other RICO claims intact. Garnett said she would allow Uber to seek to revive the dismissed claim. Uber alleges in the lawsuit that "unscrupulous personal injury attorneys" were sending clients to "corrupt medical providers" for unnecessary or unrelated medical treatment in a kickback scheme designed to generate fraudulent injury claims. Two of the defendant law firms, Downtown LA Law Group and the Law Offices of Jacob Emrani, argued they were immune under a legal doctrine known as Noerr-Pennington, which stems from the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment protection of the right to petition the government. But that doctrine does not protect sham litigation, Garnett said. Uber claimed that the law firms made "false and misleading statements concerning the severity of their clients’ injuries, the necessity of the medical treatment, and the nature of the lien agreements, each of which was an 'essential element' of their claims," she wrote, adding that is enough to proceed at this stage of the litigation. An Uber spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Attorneys for Downtown LA Law Group and the Emrani law firm, which have denied wrongdoing, also did not immediately respond. In a partial loss for Uber, Garnett ordered the company to pay attorney fees to three of the defendants, including the Emrani firm and a California surgeon, even though they still have RICO claims pending against them. The judge found that Uber dropped some of its initial claims to avoid defending them against the plaintiffs' arguments that it was violating a California law against using litigation to stifle debate. The case is [USN:L6N41R1BP TEXT:"at least one of 20 such actions"] Uber and other major companies have filed invoking civil RICO provisions against plaintiffs' lawyers in U.S. federal courts over the last two years. Damages are tripled under RICO if the plaintiff wins. Uber has similar lawsuits pending against other law firms in Miami, New York and Philadelphia. Uber so far has a mixed track record in the litigation. A federal judge hearing the Philadelphia case ruled in May that a personal injury lawyer and his firm [USN:L6N41O15M TEXT:"must face"] claims by Uber and FedEx Corp (FDX.N) alleging they directed clients to medical providers in a scheme to exaggerate injuries and create false medical records. Philadelphia-based personal injury lawyer Marc Simon and his firm have denied wrongdoing. But the rideshare giant's similar RICO lawsuit against three New York law firms was [USN:L6N44E0SI TEXT:"dismissed by a federal judge last week"] who said Uber failed to show that the firms benefited from their association with the doctors, "other than from commonplace fee-sharing arrangements, client referrals, and medical testimony, not bribes." The case is Uber Technologies, Inc. v. Downtown LA Law Group LLP et al, U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, 2:25-cv-00612. item.title: Entierran en Ceuta a los primeros migrantes tras mortal avalancha en la frontera
item.description: Ante una docena de periodistas y un puñado de vecinos, un equipo de sepultureros, ataviados con monos protectores desechables y mascarillas, comenzó el viernes a enterrar a algunos de los decenas de migrantes que fallecieron hace tres semanas durante una travesía masiva hacia el enclave español de Ceuta, en el norte de África.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ante una docena de periodistas y un puñado de vecinos, un equipo de sepultureros, ataviados con monos protectores desechables y mascarillas, comenzó el viernes a enterrar a algunos de los decenas de migrantes que fallecieron hace tres semanas durante una travesía masiva hacia el enclave español de Ceuta, en el norte de África. Un clérigo musulmán recitó una breve oración mientras los trabajadores depositaban a las cuatro primeras víctimas, envueltas en bolsas mortuorias blancas, en fosas revestidas de bloques de hormigón, una junto a otra, en el cementerio musulmán de Ceuta, mientras los coches fúnebres traían más cuerpos. El director en funciones del cementerio, Said Mohammed, afirmó que el plan era enterrar alrededor de 70 cadáveres en los próximos días, a un ritmo de entre 10 y 12 entierros diarios. Aproximadamente el 95% de los fallecidos aún no han sido identificados, pero cada tumba se ha marcado con una lápida numerada por si acaso alguien reclamara el cuerpo y este fuera repatriado en el futuro, explicó. Las autoridades afirman que entre 5.000 y 8.000 personas permanecen en Ceuta después de que al menos 72.000 cruzaran desde Marruecos el 30 de julio en una avalancha que se saldó con 82 migrantes muertos en el lado español de la frontera, además de otras 14 muertes confirmadas por Marruecos. Los migrantes fueron enterrados según los ritos musulmanes, que exigen que el cuerpo se coloque orientado hacia La Meca y se cubra con tierra, explicó Mohammed. Las autoridades solo han podido identificar a seis migrantes, todos ellos hombres adultos marroquíes, según los últimos datos facilitados por el juzgado de Ceuta. Los desesperados familiares marroquíes de los migrantes desaparecidos, han estado pidiendo información en las redes sociales y presionando a los funcionarios en la frontera. Los datos dactilares de los migrantes se cotejaron con las bases de datos españolas y marroquíes y sus muestras de ADN se compararon con las de los familiares que se presentaron, explicó el teniente coronel de la Guardia Civil Carlos Atoche, que dirige la división de delitos de la policía y encabezó un equipo de nueve agentes enviado a Ceuta. Señaló que una de las principales razones del escaso número de identificaciones ha sido la dificultad de los familiares marroquíes para cruzar legalmente a Ceuta y dejar muestras de ADN en una oficina habilitada por las autoridades españolas cerca de la frontera.

item.title: US HHS launches initiative to improve response to missing autistic individuals
item.description: U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Friday launched an initiative to improve preparedness and response when autistic individuals are reported missing.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Friday launched an initiative to improve preparedness and response when autistic individuals are reported missing. Here are more details: The National Autism Missing and Endangered Person Alert Initiative will work to strengthen coordination among emergency management agencies, law enforcement, first responders, and community partners nationwide, HHS said in a statement. The initiative will also establish a national framework of best practices to address the leading causes of preventable injury and death among autistic individuals, which include accidental drowning linked to wandering and elopement. According to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, autism affects about one in 31 children in the United States. At an April 28 meeting, an interagency autism committee approved several recommendations, including enhanced screening for co-occurring medical conditions and the development of federal guidance on wandering and elopement. In addition to this initiative, the Department of Health and Human Services is releasing a broad set of coordinated actions to improve the safety, healthcare, and services available to individuals with autism across all stages of life, HHS said in its statement.

item.title: Prince Harry's wife Meghan in talks for role in Guy Ritchie's Netflix series, report says
item.description: Meghan, the wife of Britain's Prince Harry, is in advanced talks to appear in "The Gentlemen", a Netflix series directed by Guy Ritchie, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Meghan, the wife of Britain's Prince Harry, is in advanced talks to appear in "The Gentlemen", a Netflix series directed by Guy Ritchie, according to the Hollywood Reporter. The report comes after the surprise news that Harry, who stepped down from official duties in 2020, will return with Meghan and their two children to [USN:L1N44H0DC TEXT:"live in Britain"] from their current home in California. The discussions are around a part in the third series of "The Gentlemen", according to the Hollywood Reporter. A spokesperson for the couple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The first series of "The Gentlemen" was about a man who unexpectedly inherits his family's country estate, only to discover that it is at the centre of a sprawling cannabis empire and Britain's criminal underworld. The second series will appear on Netflix (NFLX.O) next month.

item.title: Regulador neerlandés multa con 966 millones de dólares a Uber por suspensión automática de conductores
item.description: La Autoridad Neerlandesa de Protección de Datos impuso una multa de 825 millones de euros (966 millones de dólares) a Uber por desactivar cuentas de conductores mediante sistemas automatizados sin informarles de manera adecuada, según una resolución del 17 de agosto a la que tuvo acceso Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Toby Sterling
item.content:encoded: La Autoridad Neerlandesa de Protección de Datos impuso una multa de 825 millones de euros (966 millones de dólares) a Uber por desactivar cuentas de conductores mediante sistemas automatizados sin informarles de manera adecuada, según una resolución del 17 de agosto a la que tuvo acceso Reuters. La sanción sería la segunda más elevada impuesta hasta la fecha en virtud del Reglamento General de Protección de Datos de la Unión Europea. Solo la supera la multa de 1.200 millones de euros impuesta a Meta (META.O) por Irlanda en 2023 por transferir ilegalmente a Estados Unidos datos de los usuarios europeos de Facebook. Uber (UBER.N) dijo que también recurriría la decisión, al igual que hizo Meta en su día. "Estamos totalmente en desacuerdo con esta decisión y con esta multa desproporcionada", dijo un portavoz, quien añadió que la empresa se toma muy en serio los derechos de los conductores y que sus políticas incluyen revisiones humanas y la posibilidad de que los conductores impugnen las suspensiones de la plataforma. La autoridad neerlandesa confirmó la decisión más tarde el viernes. "Uber ha cometido infracciones graves" al desactivar cuentas de conductores sin previo aviso ni intervención humana, dijo en un comunicado la vicepresidenta del regulador, Monique Verdier. "De un momento a otro, dejaron de tener ingresos (...) Un computador no debería tomar por sí solo decisiones que tengan consecuencias tan graves". Los reguladores europeos han impuesto multas millonarias a las grandes firmas tecnológicas estadounidenses en los últimos años en virtud de la normativa sobre privacidad, competencia y mercado digital. Meta, Google (GOOGL.O) , Apple (AAPL.O) y Amazon (AMZN.O) se enfrentan a múltiples sanciones, aunque las más sonadas suelen reducirse o anularse tras procesos de recurso que duran años. El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ha criticado estas multas y, en abril, un funcionario del Departamento de Estado dijo que constituyen la "mayor fuente de fricción" en las relaciones económicas entre Estados Unidos y la Unión Europea. Las normas del RGPD prohíben las decisiones tomadas exclusivamente por algoritmos informáticos cuando tienen un impacto significativo en la vida de las personas, al considerar que dichas decisiones requieren una revisión humana significativa y la posibilidad de impugnar la decisión. El caso contra Uber se refiere a incidentes ocurridos en Europa entre 2018 y 2022, y tiene su origen en una denuncia presentada en Francia. El caso fue tramitado por el regulador neerlandés, ya que la sede europea de Uber se encuentra en Países Bajos. Uber suspendió temporalmente las cuentas de algunos conductores sospechosos de fraude, entre otros casos, cuando sus sistemas concluyeron que habían realizado desvíos innecesarios para inflar las tarifas o habían aceptado viajes sin intención de completarlos. Uber dijo que dichas suspensiones solían ser breves y que no desactivaba de forma permanente dichas cuentas sin una revisión humana. En ocasiones, las cuentas de los conductores con bajas valoraciones de los clientes eran desactivadas de forma permanente por el sistema informático, según la agencia neerlandesa. Uber lo negó, alegando que nunca había automatizado las decisiones de desactivación permanente. La empresa señaló que una de las razones por las que considera desproporcionada la multa es que solo se vio afectado un número reducido de conductores: en 2021, 126 fueron desactivados en Europa como consecuencia de bajas valoraciones de los clientes. La agencia señaló que la multa se calculó como una fracción de la facturación anual de Uber en 2025. La organización suiza de derechos digitales PersonalData.io, que ayudó a los conductores franceses de Uber a recabar datos sobre las decisiones algorítmicas que afectaban a su trabajo, lo que finalmente condujo a la investigación neerlandesa, se mostró satisfecha con la decisión. Su fundador, Paul-Olivier Dehaye, señaló que la organización está preparando una demanda colectiva contra Uber para reclamar una indemnización para los conductores.

item.title: Supreme Court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday allowed President Donald Trump's administration to continue construction of his White House ballroom project for now, temporarily pausing a judicial order that would halt much of the development.
item.dc:creator: John Kruzel
item.content:encoded: The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday allowed President Donald Trump 's administration to continue construction of his White House ballroom project for now, temporarily pausing a judicial order that would halt much of the development. The court's action, known as an administrative stay, gives the justices additional time to consider the administration's formal request to let it continue working on the $400 million ballroom while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the project proceeds. In an August 14 filing to the Supreme Court, Justice Department lawyers echoed Trump's contention that the project is a security necessity, citing assassination attempts against the president and other recent threats. "This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," they wrote. The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation sued last year after the administration tore down the White House East Wing and began building a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom without seeking specific approval from Congress. Trump has said the ballroom will be "the greatest of its kind ever built." The project combines the above-ground ballroom with an extensive underground complex. Trump has said the project includes bomb shelters, medical facilities, shielding from drones and missiles and other security features that are "all tied together as one big, expensive and very complex unit." On August 7, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling [USN:L6N42G129 TEXT:"upheld"] U.S. District Judge Richard Leon's order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction. The order had been set to take effect on Friday. 'A TEMPORARY TENANT' "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House," and cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the D.C. Circuit's ruling stated. The district judge's order did not permanently bar construction of a ballroom. It blocked above-ground efforts while allowing below-ground construction to continue, as well as work deemed "strictly necessary" for the safety and security of the White House. In its ruling, the D.C. Circuit said national security arguments "are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card." The Justice Department said in its August 14 filing that the overall East Wing project — including both the underground facilities and the above-ground ballroom — is 65% complete. Trump has said the ballroom project is a security necessity, and has referred to the structure as a "military center" in a post on Truth Social. Trump called the D.C. Circuit's decision "horrendous" and politically motivated, and said it left him, other White House officials and visitors exposed to attack. "This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," Trump wrote. The National Trust for Historic Preservation in court papers urged the justices to turn away the administration's bid to continue with ballroom construction while litigation proceeds. "Each court to examine the question has agreed that (the Trump administration has) no unilateral legal authority — constitutional, statutory or otherwise — to build a massive ballroom on the site of the now-demolished East Wing," lawyers for the group wrote. "And each court has told (the administration) in no uncertain terms that they must stop their illegal construction unless and until they receive express approval from Congress," it wrote. The project is part of Trump's broader efforts to reshape the Washington landscape , including plans to build a 250-foot (76-meter) arch and revamp the Kennedy Center, a cultural landmark and performance center. The demolished East Wing housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater. It was originally built in 1902 during Theodore Roosevelt's presidency and greatly expanded in 1942 during Franklin Roosevelt's presidency.

item.title: Miembros de la OTAN debaten opciones para el estrecho de Ormuz sin participación de la alianza
item.description: El comandante en jefe de la OTAN convocó una videoconferencia más temprano en la semana para facilitar posibles contribuciones en apoyo de la libertad de navegación en el estrecho de Ormuz, informó su portavoz a Reuters el viernes, añadiendo que no se trata de una misión de la alianza.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El comandante en jefe de la OTAN convocó una videoconferencia más temprano en la semana para facilitar posibles contribuciones en apoyo de la libertad de navegación en el estrecho de Ormuz, informó su portavoz a Reuters el viernes, añadiendo que no se trata de una misión de la alianza. "El Cuartel General Supremo de las Potencias Aliadas en Europa organizó el miércoles 19 de agosto de 26 una reunión de los aliados interesados, a nivel de jefes de defensa, con el fin de facilitar sus posibles contribuciones para apoyar la libertad de navegación en el estrecho de Ormuz", dijo un portavoz del comandante en jefe de la alianza, el general de la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos, Alexus Grynkewich. "Para que quede claro, no se trata de una misión de la OTAN. Pero, dadas las fortalezas únicas de la OTAN en su capacidad para reunir a los aliados y comprender las capacidades que estos aportan, tiene sentido que la OTAN facilite las cosas de esta manera", añadió el portavoz. Los aliados de la OTAN han tratado de evitar una implicación directa en el conflicto con Irán, centrándose en cambio en planes ajenos a la alianza para reabrir el estrecho, por el que, antes de febrero, circulaba cerca de una quinta parte de todo el petróleo comercializado. Francia y Reino Unido han liderado los esfuerzos para formar una coalición de aproximadamente una docena de países con el fin de garantizar el paso seguro por el estrecho una vez que las tensiones se calmen o se resuelva el conflicto, aunque cualquier acuerdo a largo plazo requeriría, en última instancia, el consentimiento iraní.

item.title: Alex Jones gets Sandy Hook family's Texas verdict reduced on appeal
item.description: Conspiracy theorist Alex Jones won an appeal in one family's defamation lawsuit over his false claims that the 2012 Sandy Hook mass shooting was a hoax, reducing the judgment against him from $50 million to about $5.5 million.
item.dc:creator: Dietrich Knauth
item.content:encoded: Conspiracy theorist Alex Jones won an appeal in one family's defamation lawsuit over his false claims that the 2012 Sandy Hook mass shooting was a hoax, reducing the judgment against him from $50 million to about $5.5 million. Jones, who filed for [USN:L1N3IC0QO TEXT:"bankruptcy"] after being sued by parents of children slain in the shooting, remains on the hook for $1.4 billion in related judgments from a Connecticut court. In the Texas case, a jury awarded over $50 million to plaintiffs Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis. Heslin and Lewis said they suffered years of harassment and abuse at the hands of Jones' followers, who falsely believed they lied about their six-year-old son Jesse Lewis' death. Texas law typically caps non-economic punitive damages, which made up $45.2 million of the verdict, at $750,000 per plaintiff. A three-judge panel of the Texas Court of Appeals ruled Friday that the trial court erred by exceeding the cap, and it ordered the punitive damages to be reduced to $1.5 million. The trial court had allowed Heslin and Lewis' lawyers to amend their claims after they won a judgment on Jones' liability but before the ruling on damages. The change allowed the parents to [USN:L1N32I2PG TEXT:"successfully argue"] that the trauma over their son's death counted as a disability that would exempt them from the punitive damages cap. The appeals court ruled Friday that the parents should not have been allowed to amend their claims to include the "disability" argument, because that argument required factual findings that the jury did not make in the case. Attorneys for Jones, Heslin and Lewis did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Jones claimed for years that the [USN:L1N333267 TEXT:"2012 killing"] of 20 students and six staff members at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, was staged with actors as part of a government plot to seize Americans’ guns. He has since acknowledged the shooting occurred. Jones has also tried to challenge the punitive damages in the Connecticut case, but the state's court upheld most of those damages, and the U.S. Supreme Court [USN:S0N3V200Q TEXT:"declined to take"] Jones' appeal. The case is Jones et al. v. Heslin et al, Texas Court of Appeals for the Third District, No. 03-23-00209-CV Read more: [USN:S0N3V200Q TEXT:"US Supreme Court rejects Alex Jones' challenge to $1.4 billion defamation judgment"]

item.title: German state politician calls for EU tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, letter shows
item.description: Sebastian Lechner, the CDU state chairman of Lower Saxony, is calling for the European Union to quickly impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, a letter seen by Reuters on Friday showed.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Rinke
item.content:encoded: Sebastian Lechner, the CDU state chairman of Lower Saxony, is calling for the European Union to quickly impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, a letter seen by Reuters on Friday showed. "It is precisely these hybrids that are currently facing the greatest import pressure from Chinese automakers," Lechner told Reuters later on Friday. Lechner pointed to an [USN:L1N4290A6 TEXT:"OECD study"] showing that approximately 60% of the market share held by Chinese products abroad is attributable to subsidies, something he called a "distortion of competition" in trade policy. "We expect the European Commission and the German federal government to adjust our trade policy toward China,” the politician said. In Lower Saxony, the issue is an important one for the Wolfsburg-based Volkswagen Group (VOWG.DE) . Import duties are already in place for electric cars from China and Lechner said EU tariffs on hybrid cars from China must be imposed quickly.

item.title: US finalizes deep Colorado River water cuts to California, Nevada and Arizona
item.description: The U.S. government on Friday finalized a plan to slash water supplies to California, Nevada and Arizona to manage the drought-stricken Colorado River.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The U.S. government on Friday finalized a plan to slash water supplies to California, Nevada and Arizona to manage the drought-stricken Colorado River. The three so-called lower basin states will take around a 21 percent reduction in water from the river in 2027 and 2028, but potential cuts could nearly double in following years, according to the plan signed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. Arizona and Nevada have said any plan to double the cuts after 2028 would devastate their economies. Arizona has threatened to sue the federal government if it imposed these potential cuts as part of the new 10-year plan. Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming, the upper basin states, face no mandatory cuts under the plan. The Colorado River provides water to one in 10 Americans, irrigates land producing 15% of U.S. food output and generates power for 6 million people in seven states. In three years of failed negotiations between the seven states, upper basin states refused to take cuts, arguing they face automatic cuts in water supply due to the severe drought impacting the U.S. West. In line with a May 1 proposal made by the lower basin states, their water allocation will be reduced by a combined 1.6 million acre feet per year in both 2027 and 2028. The reductions consist of 1.25 MAF per year in mandatory cuts and an agreement by the three states to conserve 700,000 MAF over the two years to reach combined water savings in the two-year period of 3.2 MAF. However, annual mandatory cuts to the three states could almost double to 3.0 MAF per year if needed to maintain critical reservoir levels following the first two-year operating period. Any lawsuits over those potential cuts could mean more years of uncertainty. "But this is a bridge, not a permanent solution," JB Hamby, Colorado River Commissioner for California, said in a statement. "California, Arizona, and Nevada have shown that states can compromise, make difficult decisions, and reduce water use when the river demands it. But three states cannot carry the responsibility of all seven."

item.title: Cyclisme-Le double champion du monde Julian Alaphilippe annonce sa retraite
item.description: Double champion du monde de cyclisme sur route en 2020 et 2021, Julian Alaphilippe (34 ans) a annoncé vendredi sur ses réseaux sociaux son départ à la retraite.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Double champion du monde de cyclisme sur route en 2020 et 2021, Julian Alaphilippe (34 ans) a annoncé vendredi sur ses réseaux sociaux son départ à la retraite. "C’est avec une émotion particulière, que je vous écris ces quelques mots pour vous annoncer la fin de ma carrière sportive", a-t-il écrit dans une publication Instagram, accompagnée d'un carrousel de photos retraçant les plus grands moments de sa carrière. "Après avoir mûrement réfléchi, j’ai eu l’honneur de clôturer ce chapitre de ma vie, sur les Champs-Élysées en passant par Montmartre à Paris, lors de la dernière étape du Tour de France." Julian Alaphilippe a terminé le Tour de France à la 125e place du classement général. Le coureur de la Tudor Pro Cycling Team a entretenu une histoire personnelle avec la Grande Boucle, porteur du maillot jaune à plusieurs reprises et devenu l'un des chouchous du public français par son panache. Mais c'est sur les classiques, les courses d'un jour, que le Français a écrit les plus belles pages de sa carrière avec notamment une victoire sur le Monument Milan-San Remo en 2019, la Flèche wallonne en 2018, 2019 et 2021 ainsi que les Strade Bianche en 2019. Vainqueur d'étapes sur les trois grands tours, Julian Alaphilippe est parvenu à réaliser le doublé aux championnats du monde sur route, revêtant le maillot arc-en-ciel à Imola en Italie en 2020 avant de le conserver l'année suivante dans les Flandres en Belgique.

item.content:encoded: A equipe de campanha do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) anunciou nesta sexta-feira sete novos nomes que passaram a integrar o grupo que prepara o plano econômico do candidato à Presidência sob o comando da ex-presidente da Caixa Daniella Marques. Os novos integrantes incluem nomes que participaram da equipe econômica do governo Jair Bolsonaro e profissionais com atuação no mercado financeiro e na academia. Entre os nomes, passam a integrar a equipe os economistas Alexandre Messa e Vladimir Kuhl Teles, que foram respectivamente secretário de Acompanhamento Econômico e secretário-adjunto de Política Econômica no Ministério da Economia do governo Bolsonaro. Outros egressos da equipe do ex-ministro Paulo Guedes que comporão o grupo são o engenheiro Alexandre Ywata -- que chefiou as secretarias de Infraestrutura e de Produtividade e Competitividade -- e a economista Myrian Prado, que atuou na secretaria de Desestatização. A campanha anunciou ainda os nomes do economista do mercado financeiro Andrei Spacov, do economista Arilton Teixeira, com atuação acadêmica, e do assessor de investimentos Eduardo Cavendish Carvalho. "Os novos nomes irão colaborar no plano econômico, com propostas sólidas e que possam mudar a rota da economia do país", disse em nota Adolfo Sachsida, ex-ministro de Minas e Energia do governo Bolsonaro que participa da coordenação geral do plano econômico de Flávio.

item.title: NASA-led study shows some Earth microbes could survive on the moon
item.description: The moon is, to put it mildly, an inhospitable place for people and other living organisms from Earth, with its lack of breathable air, extreme temperatures and exposure to relentless space radiation and energetic particles. That is why astronauts wear spacesuits and spacecraft are built with shielding.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham
item.content:encoded: The [USN:L2N3VF06I TEXT:"moon"] is, to put it mildly, an inhospitable place for people and other living organisms from [USN:L1N3JT0ZL TEXT:"Earth"], with its lack of breathable air, extreme temperatures and exposure to relentless space radiation and energetic particles. That is why astronauts wear spacesuits and spacecraft are built with shielding. But how about the microbes that inevitably will hitchhike with astronauts during space exploration? New research led by NASA scientists looking at five forms of fungi and bacteria indicates that some of them indeed could survive for a time under certain conditions on the lunar surface — a finding that raises concerns about unintended life transfer to the moon. These microbes were tested in modeling simulations of three regions near the lunar South Pole — Nobile Rim, Connecting Ridge and de Gerlache Rim — using environmental conditions based on observations by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and data on radiation exposure. The simulations indicated that some of the microbes could survive for periods of weeks to months in certain areas — such as inside craters that remain permanently shadowed — and during particular seasons — autumn and winter, according to planetary scientist Prabal Saxena of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. The two fungi studied proved to be hardier than the three bacteria species. Aspergillus niger, a common fungal species prevalent in warmer climates and sometimes called "black mold," was the most resilient. Aspergillus flourishes in warm and damp places like bathrooms and heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems. Astronauts have found it inside the International Space Station. Experiments have shown it can even survive outside the station while in orbit. The researchers also studied several species of Fusarium, a common soil-borne fungus. "Aspergillus was the most well-suited to survive in regions of the lunar poles. Fusarium was similarly resilient, though not to the extent of Aspergillus," said Saxena, lead author of the study published this week in the journal Science Advances . THREE BACTERIA SPECIES Three bacteria species were studied: Deinococcus radiodurans, a soil-borne microbe known for withstanding cold and radiation; Staphylococcus aureus, often found on the skin and inside nasal passages; and Bacillus subtilis, found in soil, vegetation and the human gastrointestinal tract. "The bacteria we examined were less resilient to ultraviolet radiation and consequently had less survival, with Deinococcus leading the way and Staphylococcus and Bacillus bringing up the rear," Saxena said. UV radiation and heat — lunar daytime temperatures can reach roughly 260 degrees Fahrenheit (127 degrees Celsius) — were the biggest threats, along with energetic particle radiation and the natural vacuum effects on the moon's surface. The models revealed maps of "survivable niches" as large as crater floors miles wide. Aspergillus in the models could survive even in areas with some sunlight — hence UV radiation — exposure. "Our study focused only on the survival of these cells, not their growth or reproduction," said Goddard Space Flight Center organic geochemist and study co-author Heather Graham. "But there are scenarios where cells can get buried, which would keep them warm and protected from radiation. There may also be scenarios where pockets of liquid water could form, which would potentially help the organisms grow," Graham said. These microbes could affect resources such as water — present as ice in some places on the moon — that are potentially useful for astronauts, the researchers said. The study did not look at whether lunar conditions could cause mutations making the microbes more dangerous as pathogens. "The study merely looked at cellular persistence and not mutation so we can't extend these results to include any details of future pathogenicity," Graham said. FUTURE MISSIONS The United States and China are pursuing plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since 1972 and establish longer-term moon bases. [USN:L6N40E1D9 TEXT:"NASA's Artemis program"] aims to land astronauts around the South Pole region. There is concern that contamination by Earth microbes might skew scientific understanding of the moon. "We found that the lunar South Pole and North Pole possess significant regions that may allow common human-associated microbes to survive long enough to impact scientific operations and exploration," Saxena said. Bringing microbes along on space journeys may be unavoidable, with human bodies naturally rife with them. "When we say unintended life transfer, we mean humans unintentionally depositing microbes on to the lunar surface through their spacesuits, a tool or a machine," Graham said. "Hardiness of these organisms means they can affect future sample analyses to help us understand things like chemical makeup of the regolith (lunar surface material) or the presence of certain organic molecules. Contamination is unavoidable, so we need to track what we're bringing with us so that we can later distinguish lunar chemistry from stuff we brought from Earth," Graham said.

item.title: Migrants flown to Equatorial Guinea after resisting Liberia deportation under Trump deal, sources say
item.description: Five people who the U.S. attempted to deport to Liberia this week resisted getting off the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea, another African country to which the Trump administration is removing migrants it cannot legally send home, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Robbie Corey-Boulet
item.content:encoded: Five people who the U.S. attempted to deport to Liberia this week resisted getting off the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea, another African country to which the Trump administration is removing migrants it cannot legally send home, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. The incident represents an early snag in Washington's plan to send up to 1,200 so-called third-country deportees to Liberia, one of the largest such deals it has struck in Africa despite criticism from immigrants' rights advocates. Third-country deportees have, in most cases, obtained legal protection against repatriation after U.S. immigration judges ruled they risked torture or other abuses in their home countries. [USN:L6N44H0RE TEXT:"Liberia"] announced on Tuesday that it had agreed to receive deportees and that the first group of 20 would arrive on Thursday. But a Liberian official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, told Reuters on Friday that only 15 deportees disembarked. At least five others - three Cuban men, one Brazilian man and one Cameroonian woman - refused to get off the plane in Liberia, according to three sources familiar with the incident, one of whom was a Honduran deportee on the flight. Authorities then told them they would be flown to the U.S., but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said. Liberia's information ministry did not respond to a request for comment on Friday. The five deportees are now being held with more than 30 other migrants who the Trump administration had previously sent to Equatorial Guinea under a deal that, like others in Africa, has been denounced by human rights groups and advocates who say many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated. The State Department on Friday said it remained "unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America's border security". A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said all the migrants "were deported to a safe third country", adding, "If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period". 40 DEPORTEES HELD IN EQUATORIAL GUINEA, SOURCES SAY The plane carrying the deportees arrived in Monrovia at 12:45 p.m. (1245 GMT) on Thursday after taking off from Louisiana and stopping in Dakar, Senegal, according to the ICE Flight Monitor managed by Human Rights First. It then departed for Malabo arriving at 8:50 p.m. (1950 GMT), according to the ICE Flight Monitor. There are now 40 deportees detained at a decommissioned hotel in Malabo, according to Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian migrant who arrived there four months ago. Conditions at the hotel are grim, characterized by "inadequate medical care", "severe psychological distress" and denial of legal assistance, according to a statement published last month by five rights groups, including Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta and EG Justice. "The Trump Administration is using these deportation agreements to shuffle people around to different countries like objects," said Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta. Equatorial Guinea's government did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

item.title: França alerta sobre 300 mil preservativos potencialmente inseguros
item.description: Órgãos franceses das áreas de saúde e de combate à fraude emitiram nesta sexta-feira um alerta contra dezenas de milhares de preservativos potencialmente inseguros vendidos na internet, em lojas e farmácias.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Órgãos franceses das áreas de saúde e de combate à fraude emitiram nesta sexta-feira um alerta contra dezenas de milhares de preservativos potencialmente inseguros vendidos na internet, em lojas e farmácias. As agências recolheram cerca de 260 mil preservativos vendidos em farmácias e lojas após testes laboratoriais constatarem que dois produtos apresentavam risco de rompimento ou a presença de perfurações, informaram em comunicado. Elas recomendaram que as pessoas que utilizaram esses preservativos façam exames para detectar doenças sexualmente transmissíveis e realizem um teste de gravidez caso a menstruação não ocorra. A agência antifraude, conhecida como DGCCRF, e a agência de saúde, DGS, também identificaram 30 linhas de preservativos listadas em plataformas de comércio eletrônico que não possuíam o selo de conformidade da UE nem rotulagem em francês. Dessas, cerca de 1.000 caixas, contendo mais de 40.000 preservativos, já haviam sido vendidas, informou o comunicado, acrescentando que as plataformas concordaram em remover os anúncios. O alerta incluiu uma lista de marcas de preservativos não conformes, incluindo duas fabricadas pela empresa japonesa Okamoto Industries (5122.T) e as marcas francesas My Lubie e Friday Bae, entre outras. O diretor-executivo da My Lubie, Pierre Lagache, disse à Reuters que o recall envolveu apenas um lote que apresentou resultado negativo nos testes, embora testes de acompanhamento no mesmo lote tenham demonstrado conformidade. “Estamos falando de um dispositivo médico: ao menor sinal de dúvida, retiramos do mercado sem esperar”, disse ele. “A My Lubie recolheu esse lote por iniciativa própria, como medida de precaução, mesmo que as próprias análises do fabricante não tenham encontrado nenhuma não conformidade. Apenas um lote foi afetado, nenhum outro produto da nossa linha, e até o momento nenhum dano nos foi relatado.” A Okamoto Industries e a Friday Bae não responderam imediatamente a solicitações separadas da Reuters por comentários.

item.title: What El Niño's return means for the Panama Canal — and global trade
item.description: The Panama Canal Authority walked back a previous pledge to not limit passage as it gears up for a longer-than-usual El Niño season.
item.dc:creator: Stefanie Eschenbacher, Elida Moreno
item.content:encoded: Just two years after the worst drought in the Panama Canal's history forced ships to wait weeks for passage and triggered multi-million-dollar bidding wars for transit slots, El Niño is again threatening the rainfall that feeds the waterway. With El Niño strengthening and reservoirs shrinking, the industry is bracing for a repeat of the disruption at one of the world's most important waterways — and some ships are already taking long detours via Africa. On Thursday, the Panama Canal Authority walked back a previous pledge to not limit passage as it gears up for a longer-than-usual El Niño season. 1. Where does the canal get its water? Unlike the Suez Canal in Egypt, the Panama Canal relies on fresh water to operate three sets of locks that allow ships to cross between the Pacific and Atlantic oceans through an 80-km (50-mile) artificial waterway. Operations depend on two man-made reservoirs, Gatún and Alajuela lakes, which release millions of liters of water with each transit to raise and lower ships through the gravity-fed, century-old locks. 2. Why does El Niño matter for the Panama Canal? Warming water half a world away in the Pacific Ocean can weaken the winds that bring rain to Panama — starving the reservoirs. Samuel Muñoz, an associate professor of civil and environmental engineering at Northeastern University, said that when reservoirs run low, the canal authority must cut the number of ships it allows through to conserve water — a reduction that "creates shipping disruptions that ripple through the global economic system." 3. Why are these water sources vulnerable? Since May, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute's monitoring network in Panama has recorded [USN:L1N4480TN TEXT:"some of the hottest air temperatures"] since monitoring began, with May, June and July each posting record or near-record monthly averages. "Rainfall during the same period in most of Panama was well below average," said Steven Paton, who runs the monitoring network, adding that some stations are reporting record or near-record low values, particularly around the canal. 4. How is the Panama Canal Authority responding? The Panama Canal Authority will [USN:S0N3PP05D TEXT:"start capping daily transit slots"] at 34 vessels starting September 4 and reduce the number to 32 as of September 15. However, projections are for water levels to drop further as El Niño goes on, which could lead the authority to tighten again. It echoes the 2023-24 measures, when drought cut daily transits to as few as 22 ships, according to official figures. The canal registered an average of 34 to 35 daily transits for the fiscal year of 2026, which runs from October to September. 5. How does this impact shipping? After reports that one tanker paid more than $4 million for priority passage, the Panama Canal Authority, without giving further details, acknowledged that "some ships which transited recently have paid amounts exceeding one million dollars at auction to meet their specific market needs." 6. What alternatives are there? Rohit Rathod, a senior oil market analyst at Vortexa, said that without long-term slot packages or deep auction budgets, many shippers are taking the long way around Africa instead. So far this August, roughly half of gas carriers heading to Asia have chosen the Cape of Good Hope over the Panama Canal, he said, adding that this is the highest share in a decade. The tradeoff is steep: a large gas tanker sailing from Houston to Japan takes about 26 days through the Panama Canal — but 45 days around the Cape of Good Hope. 7. What long-term solutions are being explored? Panama is weighing a longer-term fix: a new reservoir at Río Indio, which the Panama Canal Authority says would secure water for more than half the population and the canal's operation for the next 50 years, while improving conditions in nearby communities. Resistance comes from environmental activists, who were instrumental in blocking First Quantum's mining contract; some argue the reservoir is not necessary and point to alternatives such as Lake Bayano. 8. How does this El Niño compare to earlier ones? In its forecast issued last week, the Climate Prediction Center of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said that El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a [USN:FWN44A1C6 TEXT:""very strong" event"] during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. Clarksons Securities said in a research note this week that "El Niño is now emerging as a key risk" for a sector already grappling with capacity constraints and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

item.title: Why a defense lawyer went on the offensive in an Oregon robocall lawsuit
item.description: Most defense lawyers consider it a success if their adversary agrees to drop a lawsuit and move on.
item.dc:creator: Sara Randazzo
item.content:encoded: Most defense lawyers consider it a success if their adversary agrees to drop a lawsuit and move on. But when a plaintiff tried to withdraw a consumer lawsuit against attorney Ryan Watstein's insurance client, he urged an Oregon federal judge to keep the case alive. Watstein in court filings had laid out in dramatic detail why he believes serial plaintiffs and their lawyers have abused the class action system to make millions of dollars off a 1991 federal law meant to stop spam phone calls. He argued that the other side only wanted out of the case to avoid further scrutiny. Before letting plaintiff Chet Wilson dismiss the case, Watstein told the judge this week, he should be able to probe for documents and depose witnesses to try to unravel the scheme. He alleges Wilson deliberately purchased a phone number to lure spam calls, and that a web of attorneys is pressing extortionate settlement demands under contingency arrangements that promise them 90% of any recoveries in a wave of similar cases. Wilson's lawyers deny any wrongdoing and insist they and their client are just trying to stop illegal robocalls. It all came to a head Wednesday at a hearing in front of Chief U.S. District Judge Michael McShane in Oregon, who expressed deep skepticism about the sincerity of Wilson’s intentions. The judge wondered aloud whether any criminal fraud was taking place and why no other defense lawyer had ever publicly pushed back rather than reaching quick settlements. “Mr. Wilson and the lawyers who represent him are making a cottage industry out of this,” McShane said, before chiding Wilson’s attorney for making it sound like his client didn’t want to receive the spam calls. “Please don’t take me for an idiot up here.” DIALING FOR DOLLARS Watstein's campaign targets [USN:L1N39Q24L TEXT:"litigation stemming from"] the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, or TCPA, enacted by Congress to protect consumers against unwanted robocalls and junk faxes. It's expanded to include modern-day annoyances like spam text messages. Under the law, aggrieved consumers can sue the source of spam calls and collect between $500 and $1,500 per violation. Wilson, an Oregon resident who acquired a number ending 999-9999, has filed more than 80 such TCPA lawsuits in recent years, all as proposed class actions. While some defendants have settled, he met resistance when suing Watstein's client, Freeway Insurance Services of America. Wilson accused the insurer of texting him advertisements despite being on the national do-not-call registry. But in court filings, Watstein detailed how he believes a network of law firms around the country work with serial plaintiffs to gin up TCPA cases, including by using VPNs to enter numbers into online forms that lead to the spam calls. At the heart of his allegations is a small D.C. legal shop called the Heidarpour Law Firm, which serves as a lead generator and then passes off clients to law firms that file the TCPA class actions. The Heidarpour firm has attracted some prior scrutiny from TCPA defendants, and Watstein was able to leverage information from hundreds of other cases defended by his firm and others to make his arguments. Contracts involving Heidarpour that have emerged in court filings show that when the firm and its partner law firms settle a case, their clients are limited to recovering what a court could award under the TCPA's statutory cap, while the lawyers split the rest, which is often multiples more than that. Clients also agree to give the firm power of attorney to settle and pursue claims on their behalf and to reimburse Heidarpour for expenses if they ever want to fire them, the documents show, which Watstein argues makes it difficult for anyone unhappy with the arrangement to walk away. "This scheme results in millions of dollars in individual settlements," Watstein, the co-founder of Georgia litigation boutique Watstein Terepka, said at Wednesday's hearing. While the full scope of Wilson's settlements isn't clear, Watstein mentioned another serial TCPA plaintiff who settled 18 cases for $633,500, with almost 90% going to attorneys. The Heidarpour firm didn't respond to a request for comment. UNDER SCRUTINY The number of TCPA lawsuits has been on the rise in recent years. There were 1,532 TCPA lawsuits filed in the first half of the year, according to litigation analytics firm WebRecon, up 34% from last year. Serial plaintiffs drove more than half of all TCPA litigation last year, according to risk management consulting firm CompliancePoint, filing an average of 3.6 cases each. Heidarpour, whose website lists just one lawyer, isn't Wilson's counsel of record in the Oregon case. But when Watstein filed a subpoena against the firm in D.C. federal court, suspecting its involvement, the firm hired a high-powered team from Milbank to defend against it. In a filing, Milbank partner and former acting U.S. solicitor general Neal Katyal argues the accusations against the Heidarpour firm are meritless. The firm doesn’t “manufacture” spam calls or texts on behalf of its clients, Katyal says, and despite the “power of attorney” provision, the firm doesn’t resolve claims without proper client sign-off. The firm called Watstein’s claims “hyperbolic allegations” that don’t justify “the broad ranging fishing expedition” found in the subpoena. Katyal did not respond to requests for comment. Beyond his focus on Heidarpour, Watstein also argued that the plaintiff in the Oregon case, Wilson, isn’t fit to serve as a class representative in this or any case. At the hearing and in court filings, he pointed to antisemitic and racist comments Wilson has repeatedly made online. Andrew Perrong, an attorney for Wilson, said in court he couldn’t defend the comments but that they shouldn’t make him ineligible to be a class representative. In court, Perrong said Wilson had the unique phone number long before he started filing lawsuits, and that, "We bring every case intending to pursue class certification.” Perrong, based in Pennsylvania, was himself a serial TCPA plaintiff before he went to law school. Perrong didn't respond to a request for comment. In the end, Watstein’s gambit paid off. Speaking from the bench, McShane said he would issue a ruling denying class certification, finding Wilson unfit to serve as a fiduciary in a class action. He also refused to dismiss the case until the defense gathers more information from Wilson and Heidarpour about their relationship. The decision will impact a dozen or so other TCPA lawsuits filed by Wilson in Oregon federal court, including some that have recently settled. McShane concluded that robust discovery is needed “to determine exactly what is going on.”
